sec.title: Background
sec.p: Urachal carcinoma (UrC) constitutes a rare and biologically distinct adenocarcinoma for which no standardised therapeutic regimen currently exists. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combined therapy with camrelizumab, a humanised monoclonal anti programmed death-1 (PD-1) antibody, plus apatinib, a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) inhibitor, in patients with advanced UrC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: RUN-SC-0102 is an open-label, single-arm, phase 2, multicohort trial that followed a Simon's two-stage MiniMax design and enrolled participants with rare cancer types. Here, we report the urachal cancer cohort, which enrolled patients across two centres in China (Shanghai, Beijing) with histologically confirmed UrC who were refractory to at least one line of systemic chemotherapy. Patients with prior exposure to PD-1/PD-L1 or VEGF-targeted agents were ineligible for enrolment. Participants received camrelizumab (200 mg; intravenous) once every 3 weeks and apatinib (250 mg; oral). The primary endpoint was the objective response rate (ORR). Secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), duration of response (DoR), disease control rate (DCR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), and safety. Efficacy analysis was performed in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population. Safety analyses were performed on all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment. This trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400086153.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: Between June 1, 2024, and Jan 31, 2025, 20 patients with UrC were enrolled. As of data cutoff (Sept 30, 2025), the ORR was 40% (95% CI 19.8–63.1) and the CBR was 50% (95% CI 27.2–72.8). Median DoR was 7.5 months (95% CI 7.0–not reached) and median PFS was 5.5 months, (95% CI 3–not reached). The DCR was 95% (95% CI 79.2–99.2), comprising 8 partial responses (PR) and 11 stable diseases (SD) as best overall response. Median OS was not reached, with a median follow-up duration of 13.6 months (9.9–not reached). Nine patients (45%) experienced grade 3 and 4 adverse events. No grade 5 toxicities were observed.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: As the first reported trial of its kind in advanced urachal carcinoma, this study demonstrates that combined PD-1 and VEGFR inhibitor therapy is well tolerated and clinically active, warranting further investigation in biomarker-enriched, adequately powered trials.

sec.title: Evidence before this study
sec.p: Urachal carcinoma (UrC) is a rare adenocarcinoma originating from the urachal remnant, accounting for <1% of all bladder malignancies. Current systemic treatment strategies are adapted from colorectal cancer regimens. Prior to this study, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, CNKI, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry for relevant papers published between database inception and May 31, 2024, with no language restrictions. Search terms included Medical Subject Headings and free-text words related to “urachal carcinoma,” “PD-1/PD-L1,” “camrelizumab,” “apatinib,” “VEGFR inhibitor,” and “immunotherapy.” This search yielded only retrospective case series and isolated reports. These studies suggest that immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) monotherapy has limited efficacy, potentially due to a tumour microenvironment characterised by low PD-L1 expression. One small, retrospective case series (n = 12) of patients previously treated with platinum-based chemotherapy reported a median progression-free survival of only 2.85 months with various subsequent therapies, including ICI monotherapy. The available evidence indicated minimal activity of monotherapy and a need for rational combination strategies. No prospective trials had evaluated the combination of ICIs with anti-angiogenic therapy in advanced urachal carcinoma.

sec.title: Added value of this study
sec.p: To our knowledge, this is the first prospective phase 2 trial to evaluate the combination of the PD-1 inhibitor camrelizumab and the VEGFR-2 inhibitor apatinib in patients with advanced, chemotherapy-refractory urachal carcinoma. Our results demonstrate that this combination regimen is feasible and exhibits promising antitumour activity, with an objective response rate of 40% (95% CI 19.8–63.1). The median PFS was 5.5 months (3.0–not evaluable). The median overall survival (OS) was not reached at a median follow-up of 13.6 months (9.9–not reached). These outcomes compare promising with historical data on second-line chemotherapy. In addition, our findings demonstrate a comprehensive safety profile of this regimen in this unique patient population, highlighting manageable hepatotoxicity as a key consideration for clinical management.

sec.title: Implications of all the available evidence
sec.p: The collective evidence from prior retrospective analyses and the present prospective trial indicates that combined PD-1 and VEGFR inhibition represents a potentially promising therapeutic strategy for advanced urachal carcinoma, given the limited efficacy of historical ICI monotherapy and chemotherapy in this population, though direct comparative trials are lacking. These findings support a new, active salvage treatment option for this orphan disease. In clinical practice, vigilant monitoring and proactive management of liver function are recommended due to the observed hepatotoxicity. Future research should focus on validating these results in larger, optimally designed trials and should explore predictive biomarkers to identify patients who are most likely to benefit from this immunotherapeutic combination.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Urachal cancer, UrC, was first described by Begg in 1931.1 UrC is an exceedingly rare adenocarcinoma, accounting for less than 1% of all bladder neoplasms.2,3 Anatomically, the urachus is the fibrous remnant of the allantois, persisting postnatally as the median umbilical ligament. This structure extends from the bladder dome to the umbilicus but has no physiological function in postnatal life.4 UrC typically originates along the serosal surface of the bladder dome. Due to their extravesical and extraperitoneal location, they often remain asymptomatic in the early stages, leading to delayed diagnosis. As a result, most cases are identified at advanced stages, frequently presenting with local invasion or metastatic spread.5

Given its rarity, the existing literature on this condition mainly consists of retrospective case series analyses.6, 7, 8 A recent comprehensive review9 summarised current clinical, diagnostic, and therapeutic advances, including emerging prospective trials, such as the SMART (NCT06161532)10 and the E-VIRTUE (NCT06041503)11 studies. Notably, Park et al. reported the first prospective data from the ULTIMA trial, a Korean multi-centre phase II study evaluating modified FOLFIRINOX as first-line therapy for advanced UrC, which demonstrated promising objective response rates and progression-free survival.12 Nevertheless, the adverse toxicities associated with chemotherapeutic drugs substantially compromise patient compliance and treatment adherence, particularly among elderly populations. Consequently, the development of novel therapeutic strategies for patients with advanced UrC following chemotherapy failure remains an unmet clinical need.

In recent years, the advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has substantially expanded systemic treatment options beyond traditional chemotherapy for cancer. Although ICIs have gained regulatory approval across various malignancies, available retrospective data suggest limited efficacy of ICI monotherapy in UrC.13,14 Consequently, synergistic combinations of PD-1 inhibitors with other therapeutic modalities have emerged as promising strategies.15,16 Camrelizumab is a fully humanised, high-affinity monoclonal antibody that binds to PD-1. Apatinib, registered with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA) as rivoceranib, selectively inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR-2) and showed promising activity against cancer in several reports.17,18 There has been substantial evidence that the combination of camrelizumab and apatinib has a significant synergistic anticancer effect in various kinds of solid tumours.18 Both agents and their combination regimen have received regulatory approval in China, while pre-marketing regulatory reviews are currently underway in other countries.

But less is known about the role of this combination in patients with advanced UrC. As a part of a phase II, multicohort, multicentre trial including 11 cohorts, the present study was designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of camrelizumab in combination with apatinib in one cohort of patients with advanced UrC.

sec.title: Study design and ethics
sec.p: RUN-SC-0102 is a part of an open-label, single-arm, phase 2, multicentre, multicohort trial evaluating camrelizumab plus apatinib in patients with rare cancer types in across multiple sites in China. Here, we report the efficacy and safety of the combination among UrC cohort.

The trial was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Shanghai Cancer Centre, Fudan University (Shanghai) and Huanxing Cancer Hospital (Beijing) with approval number 2405296-3. All participants provided written informed consent. The trial was prospectively registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400086153). The study protocol is available in the Supplementary Materials (Supplementary File 2).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: In the present UrC cohort, key inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) patients with histologically confirmed UrC by experienced pathologist following those of Dhillon et al.19 (tumour in the dome or elsewhere in the midline of the bladder, sharp demarcation between the tumour and the surface epithelium, and absence of primary adenocarcinoma of another organ). (2) patients with locally advanced, recurrent, or metastatic disease after at least one line of systemic chemotherapy. (3) patients with no prior exposure to PD-1/PD-L1 or VEGF-targeted agents. (4) patients were aged ≥18 years and had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–1. (5) patients with at least one measurable lesion per RECIST criteria (non-lymph node lesions with a long diameter ≥10 mm or lymph node lesions with a short diameter ≥15 mm on CT scan). Additionally, patients were required to have an estimated life expectancy of ≥3 months, agreed to use medically approved contraception during the study and for at least 120 days after the last dose, and demonstrate the ability to comply with the study visit schedule and protocol requirements.

Exclusion criteria included patients with severe or uncontrolled medical conditions, major surgery or significant traumatic injury within 28 days prior to study treatment, unresolved wounds or fractures, severe hypersensitivity reactions to monoclonal antibodies, known allergies to study drug components, participation in other clinical trials within 4 weeks prior to study initiation, history of severe allergies, bleeding disorders or ongoing thrombolytic therapy, history of substance abuse or psychiatric disorders, or any condition deemed by the investigator to compromise patient safety or interfere with study completion.

Sex of the participants was determined by review of medical records and clinical documentation at enrolment. All participants were categorised as male or female based on biological sex assigned at birth. Gender identity was not assessed.
Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are summarised in the protocol (Supplementary File 2).

sec.title: Randomisation and masking
sec.p: This single-arm study involved no randomisation. The open-label design meant no masking of intervention or outcome assessment was performed.

sec.title: Study treatment
sec.p: Apatinib 250 mg was administered orally once daily and camrelizumab 200 mg was administered intravenously once every 3 weeks, until disease progression, death, unacceptable toxicities, or at the patient's request.

Dose modifications of camrelizumab were not permitted. In patients demonstrating adequate tolerance to apatinib, the dose may be escalated to 500 mg once daily. Conversely, if apatinib-related toxicities arise, the dose may be reduced by instituting an every-other-day schedule (one day on, one day off), as clinically indicated.
Details of dose modifications and supportive measures are provided in the protocol (Supplementary File 2).

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: Tumour responses were assessed by independent radiologists according to RECIST version 1.1 at the start of each 6-week cycle, with additional investigator review at each treatment visit. Adverse event (AE) data were collected up to 30 days after treatment discontinuation, and immune-related AE (irAE) data up to 90 days after the last dose of camrelizumab. Severity was graded using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 (NCI-CTCAE v5.0).

sec.title: Exploratory analysis
sec.p: The immunohistochemical analysis of programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1; antibody: CST13684) expression was conducted and evaluated by certified pathologists. PD-L1 protein expression was determined using the combined positive score (CPS), defined as the number of PD-L1–stained cells divided by the total number of viable tumour cells and multiplied by 100. We set a threshold for CPS≥ 10 as PD-L1 positive.

Whole-exome sequencing (Illumina sequencing platform) was performed to calculate the tumour mutational burden (TMB) score, defined as the number of somatic nonsynonymous mutations per megabase. We set a threshold for TMB≥ 10 mutations/megabase (mut/Mb) as TMB high.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the ORR, defined as the proportion of patients with complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) according to RECIST v1.1. Secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or death from any cause; overall survival (OS), defined as the survival time until death from any cause; duration of response (DoR), defined as the time from the first evidence of response to disease progression or death; disease control rate (DCR), defined as the proportion of patients who achieved CR, PR, or stable disease; clinical benefit rate (CBR), defined as the proportion of patients who achieved CR, PR, or more than 6 months stable disease; and safety evaluation.
Efficacy analysis was performed in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population. Safety analyses were performed on all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: This trial followed a Simon's MiniMax two-stage design to evaluate preliminary antitumour activity. The design assumed an unacceptable objective response rate (ORR) of 10% and a desirable ORR of 35%, with 80% power and a one-sided significance level (α) of 0.05. In stage 1, 11 patients were enrolled; if 2 or more objective responses were observed, the trial would proceed to stage 2 with enrolment of an additional 7 patients, yielding a planned total sample size of 18. The regimen would be considered promising if 5 or more objective responses were observed across both stages combined.

The primary endpoint (ORR) and exact 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method, chosen for its exact coverage of binomial proportions in small samples. DoR, PFS, and OS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with 95% CIs for medians calculated using the Brookmeyer–Crowley method. Other clinical outcomes, demographic characteristics, and safety data were summarised descriptively.

All prespecified analyses (primary and secondary endpoints, exploratory biomarker subgroup analyses) were defined in the protocol. In a post-hoc analysis, we calculated ORR and PFS among male and female patients, respectively. No other formal sensitivity or comparative analyses were performed, as the limited sample size (11 male and 9 female patients) precluded meaningful statistical comparisons without substantially compromising reliability.
All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 8.0.2 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA) and RStudio version 4.2.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

sec.title: Role of the funding source
sec.p: No funding was received for this work.

sec.title: Participant and disease characteristics
sec.p: Between June 1, 2024, and Jan 31, 2025, 22 patients were assessed for eligibility. Per design, 11 patients were enrolled in stage 1; with four confirmed responses exceeding the ≥2 threshold, the trial proceeded to stage 2. During the administrative transition between stages, 2 additional patients who had completed screening and informed consent were enrolled before the stage 2 stopping boundary was formally activated. These patients were retained in the intention-to-treat population per protocol-defined full analysis set criteria, yielding a final sample size of 20 (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Flowchart of patient enrolment and study design. Between June 1, 2024 and January 31, 2025, 22 patients with advanced urachal carcinoma (UrC) were assessed for eligibility. Two were excluded (one declined informed consent, one had no measurable disease), and 11 were enrolled in stage 1. Four confirmed partial responses (PR) were observed, exceeding the pre-specified threshold of ≥2 responses required to proceed to stage 2. Nine additional patients were enrolled in stage 2 (7 per protocol plus 2 during the administrative transition period), yielding a total intention-to-treat population of 20. At the data cut-off (30 September 2025), 16 patients had discontinued treatment (15 due to disease progression, 1 due to adverse events) and 4 remained on treatment.

sec.p: Of the 20 enrolled patients, 11 (55%) were male and 9 (45%) were female. All had prior bladder surgery (65% radical cystectomy) and systemic chemotherapy (70% ≥ 2 prior lines). Histological subtypes were non-mucinous adenocarcinoma (60%), mucinous (35%), and signet ring cell (5%). Most patients (85%) had peritoneal metastases. Baseline carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and carbohydrate antigen (CA19-9) were elevated positive in 55% and 35%, respectively. PD-L1 positivity and TMB were assessable in only 90% and 20% of patients. The baseline characteristics of the population are summarised in Table 1. For the detailed chemotherapy regimens, it is provided in Supplementary Table S1.

sec.p: At data cutoff (Sept 30, 2025), the median follow-up was 13.6 months. 16 patients (80%) discontinued the study treatment, with 15 developing disease progression and one experiencing unacceptable AE (liver dysfunction).

sec.title: Antitumour activity
sec.p: Among the 11 patients enrolled in Stage 1, confirmed responses were observed in 4, prompting continuation to Stage 2. Per protocol, 7 additional patients were enrolled; 2 extra participants were also included, yielding an ITT population of 20.

Eight patients (40% [95% CI, 19.8–63.1]) achieved a confirmed objective response, with no CR and 8 PRs (Fig. 2). Fig. 3 showed the overall treatment exposure data of patients. The DCR is 95% (95% CI 79.2–99.2), with 8 PRs and 11 SDs as the best response. Additionally, two patients achieved SD lasting ≥6 months, yielding a CBR of 50% (95% CI 27.2–72.8). The median DoR was 7.5 months (Fig. 4). Four of the 8 responders’ responses lasted for at least 6 months; and treatment of 4 responders is ongoing. One patient experienced PD 3.4 weeks after achieving PR and was therefore classified as having an unconfirmed PR. The median PFS was 5.5 months (95% CI 3–not reached). Six (30%) deaths occurred, and the median OS was not reached. The 12-months OS rate is 67.9% (95% CI 47.5%–88.3%).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: All patients experienced at least one treatment-related AE (TRAE). Grade 3–4 TRAEs were observed in 9 patients (45%), and the most common TRAEs were hypertension, dysphagia, fatigue, headache, liver dysfunction, hand-foot syndrome and nausea (Table 2). No treatment related deaths occurred.

During treatment, seven patients (35%) required one or more temporary suspensions of apatinib due to adverse events. One patient permanently discontinued treatment because of grade-4 liver dysfunction.

Four (20%) patients are still receiving the study treatment. One patient continued apatinib on an alternate-day dosing schedule after developing grade-3 hepatotoxicity. Two patients received escalation of 500 mg apatinib, while one patient further reduced the dose to 250 mgqd due to intolerance.

sec.title: Exploratory analysis
sec.p: Using CPS≥ 10 as a cutoff, three patients (15%) were PD-L1 positive, and 15 patients (75%) were PD-L1 negative. Due to the marked disparity in sample sizes (n = 3 vs. n = 15), the statistical power is critically constrained, precluding any defensible between-group comparison; consequently, a robust and reliable inference cannot be established.
Similarly, the limited number of samples with TMB data precluded a meaningful analysis of the association between TMB and ORR.

Exploratory subgroup analyses by sex showed ORR of 27.3% (3/11) in male patients and 55.6% (5/9) in female patients. PFS did not differ significantly between male and female patients (p = 0.08); however, this comparison was limited by small subgroup sizes and wide, overlapping confidence intervals. OS and DoR were not analysed by sex because the limited number of events (6 deaths overall; 8 responders overall) precluded reliable estimation in subgroups. These exploratory analyses should not be overinterpreted, and definitive conclusions regarding sex-specific efficacy cannot be drawn from this dataset.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To our knowledge, this is the first prospective study to evaluate the antitumour activity and safety of combining an ICI with a VEGFR inhibitor as salvage therapy for advanced UrC. Camrelizumab plus apatinib demonstrated encouraging efficacy and a manageable toxicity profile; however, reversible hepatic dysfunction was the predominant reason for apatinib discontinuation.

Evidence indicates that, despite the anatomical proximity of the urachus to the bladder, the pathological characteristics and gene–expression profile of UrC more closely resemble those of colorectal cancer (CRC).2,20,21 Immunohistochemical studies have further demonstrated overlaps between UrC and CRC, including CEA elevation and mucin production. Thus, systemic chemotherapy for urachal carcinoma has been derived from both urothelial carcinoma (MVAC, gemcitabine-platinum) and CRC (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI) regimens.22,23 Prospective study, such as the ULTIMA trial (NCT04611724) demonstrated modified FOLFIRINOX efficacy in the first-line setting, yet prospective evidence for salvage therapy is lacking.12 A small retrospective series of 12 post-platinum patients with UrC treated with physician-choice alternative chemotherapies, ICIs, endocrine therapy, or anti-angiogenics reported a median PFS of merely 2.85 months,24 underscoring the unmet need for active salvage regimens.

In the era of immunotherapy, ICIs targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 have been sporadically administered to patients with UrC.8,14,20 Available data are derived almost exclusively from retrospective series or isolated case reports; prospectively designed clinical trials are lacking. Importantly, accumulating evidence indicates that single-agent immune-checkpoint inhibition is largely ineffective in UrC in retrospective data, a phenomenon that may be attributable to the exceptionally low PD-L1 expression observed in tumour tissue and the prominent immune-exclusion signature characterising the tumour microenvironment (TME).13 Apolo et al. evaluated the safety and efficacy of cabozantinib plus nivolumab (CaboNivo) and CaboNivo plus ipilimumab (CaboNivoIpi) in a large cohort of patients with metastatic urothelial carcinoma and in several expansion, arms encompassing rare genitourinary tumours. Among a few patients with bladder adenocarcinoma (n = 15), CaboNivo yielded an ORR of 20% and a DCR of 80%.25

Rational combination strategies that reprogram the tumour microenvironment to augment immunotherapy are now being actively pursued across CRC. Cai et al. established a CRC animal model and demonstrated that apatinib potentiates the anti-tumour efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy by up-regulating PD-L1 expression and suppressing angiogenesis.26 More importantly, the effect combination of apatinib and camrelizumab in microsatellite instability-high (MSH) or mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) CRC was subsequently corroborated in a clinical trial.27 In microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer, where single-agent immune checkpoint inhibition has limited activity, a retrospective study indicates that apatinib may potentiate PD-1 blockade efficacy by improving the TME of MSS tumour tissues and increase the immune response to PD-1 blockades, thereby converting an immunosuppressive to an immunosupportive phenotype.28 Collectively, this combination therapy has demonstrated encouraging clinical activity across both MSH and MSS colorectal cancer, consistent with our observations in UrC. These findings further support the molecular and biological similarities between UrC and CRC.

Mechanistically, evidence has demonstrated that the appropriate administration of antiangiogenic agents (including apatinib) can normalise tumour vascular network, which could (in) directly alleviate hypoxia, promote T-cell infiltration, induce M1 macrophage polarisation, decrease the recruitment of Treg and myeloid suppressor cell, and downregulate inhibitory immune checkpoints such as PD-L1, thereby converting the tumour immune environment from immunesuppressive to immune-supportive.29, 30, 31 In addition, immunotherapy was also shown to promote tumour vascular normalisation. These pieces of evidence indicate that combining antiangiogenic agents with immunotherapy improves efficacy by creating positive feedback loops that reinforce each other.32,33 This combination has been verified to be promising in many other solid tumours.34, 35, 36 The results of this study provide preliminary evidence of the potential efficacy of this combination therapy in patients with advanced UrC.

The safety profiles of camrelizumab and apatinib in advanced UrC were consistent with those in other solid tumours.37, 38, 39 Moreover, AEs for either drug alone coincided with the respective instructions. Hypertension (65%) was the most frequent AE, which was similar to that in previous studies, with incidences of 57.6%–84.4%. Some AEs, such as hepatic toxicities, fatigue, and gastrointestinal symptoms, were probably because of combination therapy, and most of them could be resolved by apatinib dose adjustment, which suggested that these AEs were more likely caused by apatinib than by camrelizumab. Notably, permanent discontinuation in one patient and ongoing dose reduction of apatinib in another were both attributable to hepatotoxicity, underscoring the critical need for meticulous, longitudinal hepatic-function monitoring during this combination regimen.

The predictive value of PD-L1 expression and the TMB score for UrC were unclear because of the low positive rate.13 A study involving 42 UrC samples found that overall PD-L1 expression was low, with only 11.76% (n = 4) having CPS score ≥10. TMB is also insufficient to stimulate a systemic immune response.14 In this study, we tried to analyse the effect of PD-L1 and TMB on the treatment effect of patients, but the positive rates were too low to draw a clear statistical conclusion.

Among all 11 cohorts included in our study, the result in patients with advanced extramammary Paget's disease (EMPD) has been published.40 We found that it did not show clinical activity (ORR = 0) for the combination of patients with advanced EMPD. The difference in ORR between EMPD and UrC may be related to the heterogeneity of the two tumour microenvironments.

This study has several limitations. First, this was a single-arm study without a control group; the observed efficacy may reflect patient selection bias or the natural history of disease. The higher median age (62.7 years) and radical cystectomy rate (65%) compared with international literature suggest potential selection bias that may limit generalisability.22 Second, the small sample size (n = 20) and the observation that several partial responses represented modest tumour shrinkage just exceeding the 30% RECIST threshold reduce the precision and certainty of the observed effects. Third, the absence of gender identity data limits our understanding of whether gender-related factors may influence treatment experience or outcomes. Future studies should consider comprehensive sex and gender analyses, including hormone status and gender identity, where appropriate. Finally, with TMB unknown in 80% (16/20) and no serial CEA or CA19-9 measurements, the predictive and prognostic utility of these biomarkers could not be determined. Systematic molecular profiling and dynamic biomarker assessment in future studies are essential to identify predictive signatures.

In conclusion, our results support further investigation of PD-1 and VEGFR inhibitor combinations for advanced UrC. Reversible hepatotoxicity necessitates vigilant liver function monitoring. Definitive validation requires systematic predictive biomarker studies and larger, optimally designed trials.
